cells.tense: You are here, with the pen, weighing what this moment actually needs and answering from what you weighed.
cells.act: maintain the abundance by clearing what is finished
cells.ask: There's a piece of business behind you that keeps getting reopened in your head. It doesn't need another pass. For seven days, when it surfaces, notice it and go on. No closing ceremony, no final look.
cells.core:
Someone feels the weight of a moment and can act from what they feel without drowning in it — you do this. You take in what's around you, feel it fully, then decide fairly, and the deciding is steady enough to stand on. That's the shape of it. You read what's fair in a room, answer from that reading, and the answer holds.

What comes next is letting one finished matter be genuinely finished. Something behind you keeps getting reopened in your head, and it doesn't need another pass. Stop hauling it this week, without a last look. Other things in your life stay open longer, and there's no rush on those. The one you put down will show you what freed-up weight does with itself.
cells.sheetLine: You feel what's fair and act on it. Let a finished matter stay finished.
cells.verb: deciding fairly inside feeling — reading what a moment needs and letting that govern the response
cells.place: at the point where what is right meets what is felt, keeping the ledger in hand

cells.tense: You will be bracing for a verdict that hasn't come, adjusting for a fairness ruling the moment never asked for.
cells.act: lay the one step you can see, solidly
cells.ask: Where you'd normally brace, put down the solid next move you can actually see — all the way through — then stop at its end. Don't sketch what follows. The step gets finished when it gets finished.
cells.core:
Where fairness meets feeling, you're bracing for a decision before the situation calls for it. The adjusting runs past what's happening, trying to be fair to an outcome that hasn't arrived. Something genuine is driving that. It's just early, and the ones on the receiving end feel the scale resting on them.

A builder waits for the stone to be placed before leveling the next. At the spot where you'd brace, lay down the visible next move — small, actual — and finish it. Then stop. If you've already passed it by then, that counts; a finished step is the ask. Bracing loses its grip once your hands are on something solid.

cells.tense: You stood at a door already closed behind you, and the room you're judging from is one you left.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Write what happened in a situation you keep circling — who said what, what got decided, in sequence, no feeling words — on one page. Then close the page for the rest of the day.
cells.core:
Where fairness meets feeling, you've stepped back from the room. The judging still runs, but nobody's at the table making it — exchanges go one direction and you're not returning them, and the evenness you're good at doesn't reach anything you can touch. What's still well is your plain eye. It works fine from a distance, and it can come back through the door.

Start by writing out a situation you keep circling — what was said, what got decided, in sequence, no words for how any of it felt. One page. Then close it for the rest of the day. That clear writing hands the matter back to you as facts you can stand on, which is what any reckoning needs before it can start.
cells.sheetLine: You left the room. Plain facts in sequence are the way back.

cells.tense: You're already weighing what's fair in this, deciding the matter before anyone has said the case is open.
cells.act: perceive it with fresh eyes before judging
cells.ask: In the next charged moment, look at it for a beat as if you hadn't settled it yet — what's actually here, not what should happen — then make the call you would have made, a heartbeat later, on purpose.
cells.core:
You're already weighing what's fair here — reading the room and evening out what's out of proportion — and if someone asked, you'd say the situation just sorted itself. The evening-out has your hand in it. That hand doesn't get filed as yours.

There's a pause in this move you can find. Before you make the fair call, look at the moment first as if it hadn't been settled — take in what's actually here before working out what should happen — then make the call, same as you would, a heartbeat later. The pause isn't a different action. It's the same action with you standing beside it, which is the whole of what owning it means.
cells.sheetLine: You're evening things out. That work is yours.

attempts.check: The draft says the person's read of a situation is accurate — that they 'take in what's actually there.' That's the unsupported claim; the record says only that fair emotional judgment is operating or not, not that their judgment is correct this time. A reasonable reader could say: I don't actually know if I'm seeing it clearly; I only know I keep adjusting. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is a small act a person can do regardless of whether the diagnosis fits — none of them require the person to be broken or fixed. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about the person 'having a gift for fairness' — cut it; the core stays on what the capacity is doing, not what the person is worth.
